questions.q: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
questions.why: Parallel: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω. The result is always lower than the smallest branch. In series you would simply add them (9 Ω).

questions.q: A 0.02 Ω busbar joint carries 500 A. How much heat does it dissipate?
questions.why: P = I²R = 500² × 0.02 = 5,000 W. Heating grows with the square of the current, which is why loose joints at high current are a fire risk.

questions.q: A DC bus at 800 V carries 100 A. What is the power?
A battery delivers 2 MW for 3 hours. How much energy is that?
questions.why: Energy = power × time = 2 MW × 3 h = 6 MWh. MW is a rate, MWh is an amount.

questions.q: Why does a higher DC bus voltage reduce cable losses for the same power?
o: Resistance of copper falls with voltage
Current falls for the same power, and loss scales with I²
questions.why: For fixed P = VI, doubling V halves I, and the I²R loss falls to a quarter. This is the main reason utility-scale systems moved to 1,500 V DC.

questions.q: A load draws 1,000 kVA at power factor 0.8. What is the real power?
questions.why: P = S × PF = 1,000 × 0.8 = 800 kW. The remaining apparent power is reactive (600 kvar).

questions.q: In a balanced three-phase system, what is the relation between line voltage and phase voltage in a star (wye) connection?
questions.why: In a star connection the line-to-line voltage is √3 times the line-to-neutral voltage, e.g. 400 V line-to-line from 230 V phase.

questions.q: A converter injects reactive power into a weak grid. What is the typical effect on the local voltage?
questions.why: Injecting reactive power (capacitive behaviour) raises voltage at the point of connection, more strongly where the grid is weak (low short-circuit ratio).

questions.q: A 100 Ah cell is discharged at 50 A. What is the C-rate?
questions.why: C-rate = current / capacity = 50 / 100 = 0.5C, so a full discharge takes about 2 hours.

questions.q: A pack has 16 cells in series, each 3.2 V nominal and 280 Ah, with 2 such strings in parallel (16S2P). What are the pack voltage and capacity?
questions.why: Series adds voltage: 16 × 3.2 = 51.2 V. Parallel adds capacity: 2 × 280 = 560 Ah. Energy is about 28.7 kWh.

questions.q: Why is LFP often preferred over NMC for stationary storage?
o: Better thermal stability and cycle life, lower cost per cycle
Lower self-discharge by orders of magnitude
questions.why: LFP has lower energy density but a more stable olivine structure, higher onset temperature for thermal runaway and long cycle life, which matter more than weight in stationary sites.

questions.q: What does state of health (SOH) usually express?
o: Charge remaining as percent of usable capacity
Present usable capacity (or internal resistance) relative to the beginning of life
Cell temperature relative to the limit
Ratio of charge to discharge energy
questions.why: SOH tracks degradation, commonly as capacity relative to nameplate, and sometimes as resistance growth. State of charge (SOC) is the fill level.

questions.q: Which ageing mechanism happens even while the battery is idle?
questions.why: Calendar ageing (for example SEI growth) continues over time and is accelerated by high temperature and high SOC, even without cycling.

questions.q: What is the sequence that defines thermal runaway?
o: Self-heating triggers exothermic reactions that generate more heat, which accelerates the reactions
Dendrite growth then short circuit only
questions.why: Thermal runaway is a positive feedback loop: heat triggers exothermic decomposition, which releases more heat. It can propagate cell to cell.

questions.q: What is the main job of a power conversion system (PCS) in a BESS?
o: Convert between DC from the battery and AC for the grid, in both directions
questions.why: The PCS is a bidirectional inverter/rectifier: it charges the battery from AC and discharges DC into AC.

questions.q: In an IGBT inverter, which contributes to switching loss?
o: Overlap of voltage and current during turn-on and turn-off
The DC bus capacitor ESR only
questions.why: During each transition the device carries current while it blocks voltage, so energy is lost per switching event; total switching loss scales with switching frequency.

questions.q: A chiller removes 300 kW of heat and consumes 100 kW of electricity. What is its COP?
questions.why: COP = heat moved / electrical input = 300 / 100 = 3. Chillers move heat, so COP is greater than 1.

questions.q: A pump runs at half speed. Ideal power consumption changes by what factor (affinity laws)?
questions.why: Flow scales with speed, head with speed squared and power with speed cubed: (1/2)³ = 1/8. That is why variable speed drives save so much energy.

questions.q: Why is a battery container usually kept to a narrow cell temperature spread?
o: Because hotter cells age faster and imbalance leads to uneven current and SOC
questions.why: Temperature spread causes different ageing rates and resistance between cells, so the weakest cell limits the string.

questions.q: What is Coulomb counting?
o: Estimating SOC by integrating current over time
questions.why: SOC(t) = SOC(0) + (1/Q)∫I dt. It is simple but drifts because of sensor offset, so it needs periodic correction.

questions.q: Why is an extended Kalman filter often used for SOC estimation?
o: It removes the need for a current sensor
It fuses current integration with a voltage-based model, correcting drift
It linearizes the whole pack to a single resistor
questions.why: The EKF predicts SOC from current and corrects it with the terminal voltage measurement through a nonlinear battery model, balancing drift against noise.

questions.q: What is the purpose of frequency containment reserve (FCR)?
o: Fast automatic power response to frequency deviations
questions.why: FCR responds within seconds to hold frequency near 50 Hz. Batteries suit it because they can change power almost instantly.

questions.q: In many ancillary markets a battery is paid for capacity availability rather than energy. What follows?
o: It must always be fully charged
It must reserve power headroom and keep energy within bounds to deliver when called
It cannot earn other revenues ever
questions.why: Capacity payments mean being able to deliver on demand, so the operator must manage SOC so both up and down response remain possible.

questions.q: In a Modbus system, which device initiates requests?
questions.why: Modbus is request-response: the master polls and the slave replies. Modern terminology is client and server.

questions.q: What is a sensible way to treat a telemetry gap shorter than a minute when computing energy?
o: Interpolate or hold last value, and flag it as imputed
questions.why: Short gaps are usually bridged by hold or interpolation while preserving a data-quality flag so downstream calculations know it was not measured.

questions.q: A test for a disease has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity, and prevalence is 1%. Given a positive result, roughly what is the probability of disease?
questions.why: Per 10,000 people: 100 sick, 99 test positive; 9,900 healthy, 99 false positives. P = 99 / 198 = 50%. Base rates dominate (Bayes' rule).

questions.q: The standard deviation is…
o: The square root of the variance
questions.why: SD = √Var, and has the same units as the data, unlike variance.

questions.q: Two variables have zero covariance. Which statement is correct?
o: They are uncorrelated but may still be dependent
One is a function of the other, linearly
questions.why: Zero covariance only rules out linear association. For example Y = X² with symmetric X has zero covariance with X but is fully dependent.

questions.q: What does the central limit theorem state, loosely?
o: Means of many i.i.d. samples with finite variance are approximately normal
questions.why: For i.i.d. data with finite variance the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal as n grows, which justifies many confidence intervals.

questions.q: What does it mean for a time series to be (weakly) stationary?
o: Constant mean and variance, and autocovariance depends only on lag
questions.why: Weak stationarity requires time-invariant mean and variance, and autocovariance that depends only on the lag. Trend or seasonality break it.

questions.q: In a Kalman filter, what happens if you increase the process noise covariance Q?
o: The filter trusts the model more
The filter trusts new measurements more and reacts faster
questions.why: Larger Q means the model is less certain, so the Kalman gain rises and the estimate follows measurements more closely, with more noise.

questions.q: Why can shuffled k-fold cross-validation mislead on time series?
o: Future information leaks into training, inflating scores
questions.why: Neighbouring points are correlated, so random folds train on the future. Use forward-chaining (rolling origin) splits instead.

questions.q: What is the main effect of L1 regularization?
o: Shrinks weights to zero, giving sparse models
questions.why: The L1 penalty has a corner at zero, so many coefficients become exactly zero. L2 shrinks smoothly without producing zeros.

questions.q: Training error is very low and validation error is high. What does this indicate and what helps?
o: Overfitting; add regularization, data or simplify
questions.why: A large train-validation gap indicates high variance (overfitting). Remedies include more data, regularization, early stopping, or simpler models.

questions.q: For heavily imbalanced data, why is the precision-recall curve often more informative than ROC?
o: ROC's false-positive rate is diluted by the huge negative class, hiding poor precision
questions.why: With many negatives, even a tiny false-positive rate can mean many false alarms relative to true positives; precision exposes that.

questions.q: In fraud detection, missing a fraud is far worse than a false alarm. Which metric to emphasise?
questions.why: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) measures how many true cases are caught, so it should be prioritised, usually while keeping an eye on precision.

questions.q: How do random forests and gradient boosting differ in how trees are combined?
o: Forests grow trees independently and average; boosting adds trees sequentially to fix residuals
questions.why: Random forests reduce variance by averaging decorrelated deep trees. Boosting reduces bias by fitting each shallow tree to the previous errors.

questions.q: What does backpropagation compute?
o: Gradients of the loss with respect to parameters via the chain rule
questions.why: Backprop efficiently applies the chain rule to give gradients, which an optimizer such as SGD then uses to update weights.

questions.q: What does PCA find?
o: Directions of maximum variance, orthogonal to each other
questions.why: PCA finds orthogonal directions (principal components) ordered by explained variance, equivalent to eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.

questions.q: What property makes a convex problem attractive?
o: Any local minimum is a global minimum
questions.why: For a convex objective on a convex set, local optimum equals global optimum, so gradient-based methods are reliable.

questions.q: Deciding which chillers to switch on or off each hour, plus their loads, is best modelled as…
o: Gradient descent on a neural net
questions.why: On/off decisions are binary variables, while loads are continuous, with linear constraints, so MILP is the natural fit.

questions.q: What does model predictive control (MPC) do at each step?
o: Solves an optimization over a horizon, applies the first action, then repeats
questions.why: MPC solves a finite-horizon optimal control problem using a model and forecasts, applies the first move, then re-solves with new measurements (receding horizon).

questions.q: What is a confounder?
o: A variable that affects both the treatment and outcome
questions.why: A confounder creates a spurious association between treatment and outcome unless it is controlled for or randomisation breaks the link.

questions.q: What is the leakage mistake when fitting a scaler?
o: Fitting it on the full dataset before splitting
questions.why: Fit preprocessing on training data only and apply it to validation/test; otherwise test statistics leak into training.

questions.q: Why do we seed random number generators in experiments?
questions.why: A fixed seed makes stochastic steps (splits, initialisation) repeatable, so differences between runs can be attributed to changes you made.

questions.q: Which monitoring signal detects that live input data no longer resembles training data?
o: Data drift metrics such as PSI or KS test
questions.why: Drift monitoring compares live feature distributions with a reference (PSI, KS), warning before performance metrics, which need labels, can be computed.

questions.q: What does epistemic uncertainty represent?
o: Uncertainty due to limited knowledge or data, reducible with more data
questions.why: Epistemic uncertainty is about the model; aleatoric is inherent randomness. Gaussian processes and ensembles express epistemic uncertainty.

questions.q: Which describes a Gaussian process?
o: A distribution over functions defined by a mean and a kernel
questions.why: A GP places a prior over functions with covariance given by a kernel; the posterior gives predictions with uncertainty.

questions.q: What principle does empirical risk minimisation describe?
o: Minimising the average loss on the training data as a proxy for the true expected loss
questions.why: ERM picks the model with the lowest average training loss, hoping that generalises; regularisation controls the gap.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this function?
questions.why: A set lookup and insert are O(1) on average, so one pass over n items is O(n). A list would make the check O(n) and total O(n²).

questions.q: What is the time complexity?
questions.why: The inner loop runs n−i times, so total = n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2, which is O(n²).

questions.q: What is the complexity of this code?
questions.why: `x in ys` on a list scans up to m elements, performed for each of n items, so O(n·m); with m ≈ n it is O(n²). Making ys a set gives O(n).

questions.q: What is the complexity of this loop?
questions.why: The value is halved each iteration, so it takes log₂ n steps.

questions.q: What is the complexity of the following, with sizes n and m?
questions.code:
def g(a, b):
    for x in a:       # n items
        print(x)
    for y in b:       # m items
        print(y)
questions.why: The loops are sequential, not nested, so costs add: O(n + m).

questions.q: Appending to a Python list is described as amortized O(1). What does that mean?
o: Occasional resizes are expensive, but the average over many appends is constant
It's O(1) only for small lists
questions.why: Resizing copies the array occasionally, but capacity grows geometrically, so the total cost over n appends is O(n).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.code:
def add(x, bag=[]):
    bag.append(x)
    return bag

print(add(1))
print(add(2))
questions.why: The default list is created once, at function definition, and shared across calls. Use None as the default and create the list inside.

questions.q: Which is true about dictionary ordering in Python 3.7+?
questions.why: Since Python 3.7 insertion order is part of the language guarantee.

questions.q: Which is called first when creating an instance?
questions.why: `__new__` allocates and returns the instance; `__init__` then initialises it. Overriding `__new__` is needed for singletons or immutable subclasses.

questions.q: Why catch a specific exception rather than a bare `except:`?
o: A bare except also swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit and hides bugs
questions.why: Bare except catches BaseException subclasses too, such as Ctrl-C. Catch the narrowest exception you can handle.

questions.q: What does it mean for an operation to be atomic?
o: It appears to happen entirely or not at all, with no visible intermediate state
questions.why: Atomic operations cannot be observed half-done by other threads or transactions. Database commits and compare-and-swap are examples.

questions.q: In CPython, why do CPU-bound threads not run in parallel?
o: The global interpreter lock lets only one thread execute bytecode at a time
questions.why: The GIL serialises bytecode execution. Use multiprocessing (or native extensions releasing the GIL) for CPU parallelism; threads are fine for I/O waits.

questions.q: What is an idempotent operation?
o: One that can be safely repeated with the same effect as running once
One that runs in constant time
questions.why: Idempotency makes retries safe, e.g. PUT or setting a value. It matters for network calls where a response may be lost.

questions.q: What is dependency injection?
o: Passing a component's collaborators in from outside instead of creating them inside
questions.why: Injecting dependencies decouples code and makes it easy to substitute fakes in tests.

questions.q: What is a regression test for?
o: Checking that a previously fixed bug or behaviour does not return
questions.why: Regression tests lock in behaviour so later changes cannot silently break it.

questions.q: What should go in .gitignore?
o: Files you don't want tracked, like secrets, build output, virtualenvs
questions.why: Ignore generated files and anything sensitive. Secrets already committed stay in history, so rotate them.

questions.q: Which HTTP method is normally used to retrieve a resource without side effects?
questions.why: GET is safe and idempotent: it reads without changing server state.

questions.q: What does HTTP status 404 mean versus 500?
o: 404: resource not found (client side); 500: server error
questions.why: 4xx codes mean the request was at fault, 5xx mean the server failed.

questions.q: What does a foreign key do?
o: Enforces that a value in one table refers to an existing row in another table
questions.why: It maintains referential integrity, preventing orphan rows (and can control cascading deletes).

questions.q: What defines a primary key?
o: A column (or set) that uniquely identifies each row and cannot be null
questions.why: Primary keys are unique and non-null, and give rows a stable identity that foreign keys can reference.

questions.q: What is the trade-off of adding an index?
o: Faster reads on that column, but slower writes and extra storage
questions.why: Every insert, update or delete must also maintain the index, so over-indexing hurts write-heavy tables.

questions.q: Which problem does the 'read committed' isolation level prevent?
questions.why: Read committed ensures you only read committed data; non-repeatable and phantom reads can still occur.

questions.q: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
o: All rows from the left table, with matching right rows or NULLs
All rows from the right table
questions.why: Left rows are kept even when there is no match; right-side columns are NULL in that case.

questions.q: What is the purpose of normalization?
o: Reduce redundancy and update anomalies by structuring data into related tables
questions.why: Normalization stores each fact once, avoiding inconsistent updates; the cost is more joins.

questions.q: Why partition a large time-series table by time?
o: Queries on time ranges can skip irrelevant partitions and old data can be dropped cheaply
It removes the need for keys
It makes writes slower on purpose
questions.why: Partition pruning limits scanned data, and retention is a cheap partition drop instead of a massive delete.

questions.q: Why are columnar formats like Parquet good for analytics?
o: They read only the needed columns and compress well
They are always smaller than CSV by 1%
questions.why: Analytical queries touch few columns across many rows; columnar layout lets engines skip the rest and compress similar values.

questions.q: What distinguishes replication from sharding?
o: Replication copies the same data to several nodes; sharding splits data across nodes
questions.why: Replication gives availability and read scale; sharding gives write and storage scale at the cost of cross-shard complexity.
